Maximum employment is the highest level of employment that can be achieved while sustaining price stability. While these objectives are generally complementary, the consensus statement says we follow a balanced approach in promoting them when they are not. A reaction function describes how monetary policy typically responds to economic fundamentals to reach the goals. For example, when inflation is too high, monetary policymakers tend to raise interest rates to bring inflation back down. When the labor market is weak, policymakers tend to reduce interest rates to stimulate economic activity. Simple monetary policy rules capture these reactions in a stylized way. The original Taylor rule provides one reaction function that relates the federal funds rate to the equilibrium real rate, inflation, and the state of the real economy.

Explaining my thinking about policy also helps align expectations about the future. Many theoretical models used in macroeconomics posit that expectations play a crucial role in determining outcomes. In particular, being clear on the destination and the FOMC’s plan regarding how and when to get there helps anchor longer-term inflation expectations in line with our 2 percent objective, something which, in turn, makes it easier to achieve that outcome. History shows that it is very costly to restore the inflation anchor once it has been lost. I want to draw a sharp line here. A reaction function is not forward guidance. Treating the two as interchangeable can turn a well-meaning explanation of logic into the expectations of a promise. Forward guidance is a specific tool: an explicit commitment about the future path of policy, typically deployed when the federal funds rate is at the effective lower bound, like it was following the financial crisis.

For example, the Center for Inflation Research at the Reserve Bank provides daily nowcasts of inflation on the Bank’s website. The Center also produces alternative inflation measures—median CPI, trimmed-mean CPI, and median PCE inflation among them—in an attempt to remove some of the volatility from inflation measures and extract the medium-term inflation trend. As another example, the Reserve Bank researchers collect and share data from Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (or “WARN”) Act notices to capture mass layoff announcements, which research has found can help predict changes in the unemployment rate.3 [OFFICIAL] markets aggregate an enormous amount of information quickly, sometimes in mere moments after an event occurs. I pay close attention to financial conditions because they play a role in transmitting policy to the broader economy.

Higher tariff rates have been pushing up costs on the supply side. While a one-time increase in tariff rates could potentially be viewed as a one-time increase in the price level, multiple waves of tariff rate increases have resulted in a series of cost shocks. And it’s not just the supply side. Demand-side pressures coming from the AI buildout are raising prices on key computer, electronic, and high-tech components. This is raising costs for data centers, yes, but also for projects that use similar components in aviation, electricity production, and construction. When I talk with contacts across the District, I hear about additional cost pressures in health insurance, plastics, metals, grains, electricity, and other areas. Price pressures are also showing up in core services inflation excluding housing, a category that shouldn’t be especially exposed to tariffs or energy.

Trend inflation measures point in the same direction. the Reserve Bank researchers estimate that once the median and trimmed-mean inflation measures are adjusted to account for changes in skewness, trend inflation sits in the mid to high 2 percent range, in line with other statistical measures of trend inflation. Because of the breadth of inflationary pressures, my baseline forecast is that it will take some time for inflation to return to 2 percent, even with appropriate monetary policy. A leveling off or decline in energy prices would certainly help move inflation in the right direction, but the demand-side pressures are not self-correcting. They are likely to be more persistent and usually require a more restrictive policy to reign them in. During my two years at the helm of the Reserve Bank, the economy has experienced a number of upside inflation developments, and the risks still appear to be skewed in that direction.

That’s the difference between a swell that passes under the hull and a genuine shift in the current: I can look through one supply shock without changing course. I have a much harder time looking through shocks that arrive one after another. So far, long-run inflation expectations have stayed remarkably well anchored despite actual inflation being above target for more than five years, but I’m not taking that for granted. With each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risks of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy. I’m beginning to hear this from business contacts. A District retailer, tired of several supply shocks pushing up input costs, said recently that they plan to increase prices by more than their current input costs have increased.

They know there’ll be more inflation coming, they just don’t know from where. This could be a sign that an inflationary mindset is taking hold. When people expect higher prices, they make decisions with this in mind. It can become a self-fulfilling prophecy that makes it harder for monetary policy to bring inflation back down. Meanwhile, the stable labor backdrop gives me room to address these inflationary concerns. The relatively low unemployment rate of 4.2 percent has been steady since late last year and is close to my estimate of maximum employment. Other measures corroborate a stable to improving labor market. Payroll growth has picked up this year compared with that of last year. Initial claims for unemployment insurance are low, as are WARN notices of mass layoffs.

The AI buildout has created strong demand for workers in certain construction industries. District contacts report this is contributing to worker shortages and rapid wage growth in some skilled trades. Recently, I’ve also heard more reports of difficulties finding unskilled workers than I’ve heard of plans for workforce reductions. The risks to our maximum employment mandate may now be leaning toward increased tightness. More broadly, GDP growth was solid in the first half of the year and appears to have grown again at a solid pace in the third quarter. Despite high energy prices, consumer spending was strong through August. CapEx spending on data centers and associated equipment has been robust. When I speak with companies in the region, I hear that business is generally strong to booming.

My forecast calls for continued solid growth ahead. With the meaningful recent rise in yields, I see financial conditions as neutral rather than holding demand back. Strong earnings growth has supported higher equity market valuations, and corporate bond spreads are low. Market contacts report that rising bond yields reflect myriad factors such as expectations for strong growth, higher policy rates, higher energy prices, geopolitical concerns, and expanding global debt issuance. Part of this move may be a growing realization that neutral real rates are back to their pre-GFC levels, although difficulties estimating neutral rates are well known. None of this reads to me as an economy in which the crew are exhausted and the boat is taking on water. It reads, instead, as one that can handle a tighter hand on the tiller to finish the job on inflation.

Considering all the inputs that factor into my reaction function, a restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2 percent inflation. Trimming the sails through frequent smaller adjustments reduces the risks of being blown far off course, of an inflationary mindset taking hold, and of taking longer to reach the destination. As is always true, this view is conditional on circumstances. A shift in the winds can easily cause a course change. If the labor market shows convincing signs of deterioration, the path of policy would likely need to respond. Inflation that remains elevated relative to my forecast or the settling in of an inflationary mindset could require pointing the bow of monetary policy rates toward an even higher latitude.

Closing Let me close by saying that I’m not going to hand you a fixed course for how we’ll get to our destination because I don’t have one. Reaction functions are conditional. Conditionality is not a promise, but, rather, my response to shifting winds to reach the ultimate destination of maximum employment and price stability. And, importantly, to reach it in time for dinner. [OFFICIAL] you again for having me and for coming to [CITY]. I look forward to my conversation with Ellen and to your questions. Footnotes - I’m grateful to Dani Carlson, Tasia Hane, [OFFICIAL] Knotek, and Karen Mracek for assistance with these remarks.
